parsed.hook: Sonoma Mountain’s volcanic soils and high-elevation fog line give this Chardonnay its signature tension: ripe stone fruit meets razor-sharp acidity, a rare balance in California. Paul Hobbs’ Richard Dinner Vineyard block, planted in rocky loam at 1,200 feet, forces vines to dig deep, yielding grapes with concentrated flavor but no excess weight. This isn’t your buttery Napa Chard—it’s a cooler, leaner expression that drinks like a cross between Burgundy and Sonoma Coast.
parsed.wine_summary: Paul Hobbs’ Agustina Cuvée is a single-vineyard Chardonnay from the Richard Dinner estate on Sonoma Mountain, a site defined by its volcanic past. The AVA’s soils—decomposed volcanic rock mixed with clay loam—drain quickly, stressing vines just enough to produce small berries with thick skins. This, combined with the site’s elevation (400–2,295 feet), keeps acidity high even as fruit ripens fully. Hobbs’ winemaking amplifies the site: whole-cluster pressing, native yeast fermentation, and 18 months in French oak (30% new) add texture without masking the mineral core. The result is a Chardonnay that splits the difference between California’s sun-drenched richness and Burgundy’s nervy precision—a style that’s gained traction as drinkers tire of over-oaked, flabby whites.
parsed.terroir_expression: Sonoma Mountain’s geology is a story of fire and erosion. The AVA sits atop the Sonoma Volcanics formation, a mix of basalt, andesite, and tuff that erupted 3–5 million years ago. These soils, especially the rocky loam of the Richard Dinner Vineyard, force roots to struggle, reducing vigor and concentrating flavors in the grapes. The site’s elevation—above the morning fog layer but below the harshest winds—extends hang time, allowing fruit to develop complexity while retaining acidity. The wine’s signature tension—bright citrus, ripe pear, and a flinty mineral edge—comes from this interplay: volcanic soils lend a stony, almost saline note, while the cool nights (diurnal swings of 30+°F) preserve freshness. Unlike the broader Sonoma Coast, which can lean toward lean and austere, Sonoma Mountain’s warmer days and volcanic soils add a layer of ripe orchard fruit without sacrificing structure.
parsed.vinification_summary: Hobbs treats this Chardonnay like a red wine in some ways: whole-cluster pressing to extract skin contact and phenolic grip, native yeast fermentation to build texture, and 18 months in French oak (30% new) for subtle spice and creaminess. The key technical choice here is malolactic fermentation—Hobbs allows partial ML to soften the wine’s acidity without erasing its brightness. The oak regimen is restrained; the barrels are used for multiple vintages, so the toast and vanilla notes are integrated, not dominant. The result is a wine that tastes both rich and linear, with a creamy mid-palate that doesn’t tip into heaviness. This approach mirrors Hobbs’ work in Burgundy, where he’s a consultant—prioritizing site expression over winemaker signature.

parsed.insider_take: Most people assume this is a ‘Burgundy-style’ Chardonnay, but that undersells its California identity. The Agustina Cuvée is its own thing: a wine that marries Sonoma Mountain’s volcanic soils with Hobbs’ deft touch, resulting in a Chardonnay that’s richer than Meursault but more mineral than Carneros. The tradeoff? It’s not as immediately charming as a buttery Napa Chard—this wine rewards patience and attention. If you’re looking for a crowd-pleaser, skip it. If you want a Chardonnay that challenges and intrigues, it’s one of the best values in California’s premium white wine scene.
